blocks.text: Based in Ariège, the Trigone collective travels far from home, only to return. Since September, and for a year, the trio’s caravan, converted into a darkroom, has been travelling across France as part of the Réseau Lux’s Lux Tour. Marianne Thazet, Paul Baudon and Anthony Jean present À l’origine du cœur (At the Origin of the Heart) , a photographic, poetic and scientific performance that transforms a heartbeat into an image. We spoke with the three creators of the project between tour dates.
How are you feeling after this latest weekend presenting À l’origine du cœur ?

Anthony Jean: We need some time to rest after weekends like the one we just spent in Clermont-Ferrand. It was very intense, but also exhilarating and fascinating. We were fully booked for both days of performances in the Jardin Lecoq, a green space right in the city centre. I use the word “performance” because À l’origine du cœur invites people into a world of sensitivity, at the intersection of analogue photography, biology and poetry, offering them the opportunity to take a photograph with their heart. From the moment they enter the caravan, which has been converted into a darkroom, to the moment they receive a print of their heartbeat, we feel that “performance” is the appropriate term.
How long have you been travelling with this project?
Anthony Jean: Our first event was the launch of the Bicentenary of Photography at the Palais-Royal on 3 September. Since then, we’ve had five other stops, and we’re now preparing to head to Nîmes.
Marianne Thazet: The tour will end in September 2027. It will take up almost all our weekends, apart from a proper break between mid-November and mid-March.
When and how did À l’origine du cœur come about?

Paul Baudon: It was my graduation project. When we formed the collective with Marianne and Anthony, after graduating from ETPA Toulouse, where we met, we installed a mobile analogue darkroom in the caravan. We tested À l’origine du cœur at a photography festival in Toulouse and received very positive feedback. We realised that the project only really made sense when it was shared, becoming a collaborative work.
What role does each of you play in the performance?

Marianne Thazet: We need at least three people. We begin by placing electrodes on a participant’s body. I work with women and children. Paul and I are inside the caravan, while Anthony handles the process outside, welcoming participants and producing the prints.

Anthony Jean: Once the image of the heartbeat comes out of the chemical processing area, we wash it, dry it, scan it, convert it back into a positive and print it. The process takes place outdoors, in full view of everyone. People can watch us work and handle the print. They witness the entire process.
Ultimately, this is a project led by a collective that brings even more people into the collective process.

Marianne Thazet: Each of us has experienced this idea of working together in our own way for a long time, even before returning to study photography and founding Trigone. We didn’t really know what we would do within the collective, but we were convinced of the strength of this approach and our desire to pursue it.

Paul Baudon: When the three of us first came together, we were aware of the affection we had for one another, but also of our differences and how we complemented each other. We have three completely different approaches to photography, three perspectives that come together to form a whole.

Anthony Jean: We knew that being a photographer is often a solitary profession and that we needed to support one another. It made sense. We were also thinking: the press is struggling, the cultural sector is having a hard time, and selling our prints is becoming increasingly difficult. Was this the moment to focus on education and sharing our passion? Buying an old caravan from the 1970s and renovating it into a mobile analogue darkroom also made that possible. We quickly began offering courses, workshops and activities in schools. This tool has been extraordinary for the Trigone collective.
Your idea of collective work extends beyond Trigone itself.

Paul Baudon: We brought together several collectives to create the Lum Festival. This year, we decided not to continue it, but those four editions were wonderful. It was an experience built around a collective of collectives, deeply rooted in the local area. The idea was to bring a photography festival into the mountains, to a village on the Spanish border, and to install photographs in places not usually dedicated to photography, such as a chapel, a town hall, a presbytery or even a river.

Anthony Jean: What we loved about Lum was that it wasn’t the festival of any one person or particular group. There was a horizontal structure that we took great care to preserve, despite all the difficulties that involved. One very positive development is that the festival joined the Réseau Lux. It’s another new adventure that we’re very pleased to be part of.
You seem equally committed to travelling and to your roots in Ariège.

Marianne Thazet: That’s also part of the reason behind the mobile analogue darkroom. We’re very aware that choosing to live in the countryside means we can’t stay here all the time. Our work involves a great deal of travelling.

Paul Baudon: We live in one of the least populated departments in France. We ran a gallery for a year and really enjoyed organising exhibitions and engaging with audiences, but we found ourselves becoming too settled. We prefer setting off again with the caravan, travelling elsewhere, taking part in festivals, and returning from time to time. We continue to work locally and are recognised as part of the region’s photography scene.
Did the residency programme also grow out of these local roots?
Marianne Thazet: We established the residency in 2022. It’s a fairly short format: ten days in a location close to where we live.

Anthony Jean: Sometimes people tell us that the format is a little intimidating. Ten days, and the clock is ticking! It’s very concentrated and extremely intensive. Artists are given carte blanche within a territory defined by the boundaries of a municipality. Each year, we move to a different municipality within our intercommunal area. To select the candidates, we issue open calls and anonymise the applications. We don’t know the applicants’ ages or reputations, and the three of us withdraw from the selection process. We’re delighted that Stéphane Lavoué will be joining us for the 2027 residency. It’s a wonderful form of recognition. We can’t wait!
